This vignette covers the times at which growth curves reach a level of their asymptote, `timeto()`, and the maximum growth rates and their timing, `maxrate()`, for the heights of children of the Berkeley Child Guidance Study. The table of the inflection points and maximum growth rates of the growth models is in the vignette *Growth models and their parameters*.

## The Preece-Baines model

The heights of the children of `BerkeleyGrowth` (see `?BerkeleyGrowth`) are not a single sigmoid curve: their growth slows down through childhood, speeds up in the pubertal growth spurt, and stops at the adult height. Model 1 of Preece and Baines (1978) describes this with five parameters,

$$ h(t) = b_1 - \frac{2 (b_1 - b_3)}{\exp(b_4 (t - b_2)) + \exp(b_5 (t - b_2))}, $$

the adult height $b_1$, the age $b_2$ in the middle of puberty, the height $b_3$ at that age, and the rates $b_4$ and $b_5$ of growth before and during puberty. The heights were measured from 1.75 years on; the model is fitted from 2 years, first for the girls:

```{r, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4}
library(gcTMB)
library(ggplot2)
berkeley <- subset(BerkeleyGrowth, Age >= 2 & !is.na(Height))
girls <- subset(berkeley, Sex == "female")
fitg <- gcTMB(Height ~ Age, data = girls, model = "preecebaines")
summary(fitg)
ages <- data.frame(Age = seq(2, 21, by = 0.05))
ggplot(girls, aes(x = Age, y = Height)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = ID), colour = "grey70") +
  geom_line(data = cbind(ages, Height = predict(fitg, newdata = ages)), colour = "blue", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Height (cm)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Time to reach a level of the asymptote

`timeto()` gives the times at which a curve reaches a percentage of its asymptote, here the ages at which the girls reach 90%, 95% and 99% of their adult height, with standard errors by automatic differentiation. With `type = "absolute"`, the times at which the curve reaches given responses, here a height of 150 cm.

```{r}
tt <- timeto(fitg, level = c(90, 95, 99))
tt
timeto(fitg, level = 150, type = "absolute")
```

`confint()` gives Wald intervals by default, `method = "profile"` profile likelihood intervals and `method = "boot"` parametric bootstrap intervals.

```{r, message = FALSE}
confint(tt)
confint(tt, method = "profile")
```

## Maximum growth rate

`maxrate()` gives the time of the maximum growth rate (`tmax`), the maximum growth rate there (`rate`), and the proportion of total growth at that time, $f(t_m)/b_1$ (`fraction`). The standard errors are by the delta method. `confint()` gives Wald intervals by default; `method = "profile"` gives profile likelihood intervals for `tmax` and `rate`, and Wald intervals for `fraction`, and `method = "boot"` bootstrap intervals as for `timeto()`. The growth rate of the Preece-Baines curve is highest in early childhood and falls until the take-off of the pubertal growth spurt; `maxrate()` gives the peak of the spurt, the peak height velocity, and the age at which it is reached. It is close to, but not the same as, the middle of puberty $b_2$.

```{r, message = FALSE}
mr <- maxrate(fitg)
mr
confint(mr, method = "profile")
```

## Timing and maximum growth rates of boys and girls

Covariates on all five parameters give a curve for each sex, and random effects of the children on the adult height, the middle of puberty and the rate during puberty a curve for each child. The default starting values pool the boys and the girls, and are far from the curve of either sex when all five parameters differ between the sexes; the fits of each sex give better starting values, the coefficients of the boys and the differences of the girls from them:

```{r}
fitb <- gcTMB(Height ~ Age, data = subset(berkeley, Sex == "male"), model = "preecebaines")
cb <- coef(fitb)[1:5]
cg <- coef(fitg)[1:5]
```

A starting vector has one entry for each coefficient, in the order of the coefficients of the model, which `gcTMBstart()` gives with their names: for each parameter the intercept, here the boys, and the contrast of the girls. The default starting values are those of the pooled data, with the contrasts zero; the custom ones are the coefficients of the boys and the differences of the girls from them:

```{r}
default <- gcTMBstart(Height ~ Age, fform = b1 + b2 + b3 + b4 + b5 ~ Sex, data = berkeley, model = "preecebaines")
custom <- setNames(as.vector(rbind(cb, cg - cb)), names(default))
round(cbind(default, custom), 3)
```

Here the default values do not even describe the pooled data: with the boys and the girls together, the least squares fit of the starting values runs off to a step at the oldest age, $b_2 = 20$, with a huge rate $b_5$.

The custom vector is given to `start` without its names (an unnamed vector in the order of the coefficients; a vector named by parameter, e.g. `c(b4 = 0.1)`, gives the value to all the coefficients of that parameter):

```{r}
fitre <- gcTMB(Height ~ Age, fform = b1 + b2 + b3 + b4 + b5 ~ Sex, rform = b1 + b2 + b5 ~ 1 | ID,
               data = berkeley, model = "preecebaines", start = unname(custom),
               control = list(restart = TRUE))
summary(fitre)
converged(fitre)
```

With 17 parameters and strongly correlated random effects, the fit needs `control = list(restart = TRUE)` to converge (see the overview `vignette("gcTMB")`).

`timeto()` and `maxrate()` with `newdata` give the times and rates of the curves of each row, here the population curves of the sexes (`random = FALSE`):

```{r}
sexes <- data.frame(Sex = c("male", "female"))
timeto(fitre, level = c(90, 99), newdata = sexes, random = FALSE)
maxrate(fitre, newdata = sexes)
```

The girls reach the middle of puberty, the peak of their growth spurt and their adult height about two years earlier than the boys. `partest()` compares a parameter between the rows of `newdata` by Wald tests, here the middle of puberty $b_2$:

```{r}
partest(fitre, newdata = sexes, parm = "b2", adjust = "none")
```

The height and the growth rate of the population curves of the sexes, the growth rate by the differences of the predicted heights:

```{r, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4}
nd <- merge(sexes, ages)
nd$Height <- predict(fitre, newdata = nd, random = FALSE)
nd$rate <- ave(nd$Height, nd$Sex, FUN = function(h) c(NA, diff(h)) / 0.05)
curves <- rbind(data.frame(nd[, c("Sex", "Age")], value = nd$Height, panel = "Height (cm)"),
                data.frame(nd[, c("Sex", "Age")], value = nd$rate, panel = "Growth rate (cm/year)"))
ggplot(curves, aes(x = Age, y = value, colour = Sex)) +
  geom_line(na.rm = TRUE) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = NULL, colour = "Sex") +
  theme_minimal()
```

### Effects on the maximum growth rate

With `b1type = "rate"`, $b_1$ is the maximum growth rate of the curve instead of its asymptote (see *The maximum growth rate as a parameter* in the vignette *Growth models and their parameters*), so that covariates on $b_1$ are effects on the maximum growth rate. This needs a curve whose maximum growth rate is proportional to $b_1$, which is not the case for the Preece-Baines curve. The growth spurt alone, from 8 years on, is a sigmoid curve above the height reached before it, as the Chapman-Richards curve with the intercept $b_4$ estimated; with `b1type = "rate"` and the log link, $b_1$ is the peak height velocity, and the effect of the sex a ratio of the rates. Each child has random effects on the peak height velocity, on the rate $b_2$, which together with the shape $b_3$ sets the timing of the spurt, $\log(b_3)/b_2$, and on the height before the spurt. The spurt is close to a Gompertz curve, the limit of a large shape $b_3$, here about 90; the log link of $b_3$ and a restart of the optimiser from the estimates (`control = list(restart = TRUE)`) let the optimiser converge there:

```{r}
spurt <- subset(BerkeleyGrowth, Age >= 8 & !is.na(Height))
fitrr <- gcTMB(Height ~ Age, fform = b1 + b2 + b4 ~ Sex, rform = b1 + b2 + b4 ~ 1 | ID, data = spurt,
               model = "chapmanrichards", start = c(b4 = 120), fix = c(b4 = FALSE), b1type = "rate",
               link = c(b1 = "log", b3 = "log"), control = list(restart = TRUE))
summary(fitrr)
maxrate(fitrr, newdata = sexes)
```

Whether boys and girls have the same peak height velocity is a likelihood ratio test of the models with and without the sex effect on $b_1$, keeping those on $b_2$ and $b_4$:

```{r}
fitrr0 <- gcTMB(Height ~ Age, fform = b2 + b4 ~ Sex, rform = b1 + b2 + b4 ~ 1 | ID, data = spurt,
                model = "chapmanrichards", start = c(b4 = 120), fix = c(b4 = FALSE), b1type = "rate",
                link = c(b1 = "log", b3 = "log"), control = list(restart = TRUE))
anova(fitrr0, fitrr)
```

`partest()` compares the maximum growth rates between the rows of `newdata` by Wald tests (see `?partest` for the contrasts and the adjustment for multiple comparisons). With two sexes there is a single difference, girls against boys, shown here without adjustment; with the log link, the differences are log ratios of the rates, and the ratios are given as well.

```{r}
partest(fitrr, newdata = sexes, adjust = "none")
```

`predict()` with `type = "parameters"` gives the asymptote of the population curves as well. For the Chapman-Richards curve with an intercept, the asymptote is the growth above the intercept $b_4$, here the growth during the spurt above the height before it, about 50 cm, so that the adult height is $b_4$ plus the asymptote:

```{r}
pars <- predict(fitrr, newdata = sexes, type = "parameters", random = FALSE)
data.frame(Sex = sexes$Sex, peak_rate = pars[, "b1"], height_before_spurt = pars[, "b4"],
           growth_in_spurt = pars[, "asymptote"], adult_height = pars[, "b4"] + pars[, "asymptote"])
```

The adult heights agree with the asymptotes $b_1$ of the Preece-Baines curves of the sexes above.

## References

Preece, M.A. and Baines, M.J. (1978). A new family of mathematical models describing the human growth curve. *Annals of Human Biology* 5, 1--24.
